findings.title: Unconditional access to organization_context.member crashes when requester is not an org member
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs on every request, not only when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed. `organization_context.member` is None when the caller is not an org member, for example staff users or API-key/token auth where `request.user` is anonymous. If the caller is not a superuser, this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`. The default audit-log listing path, which worked before this PR, then returns a 500 for those callers. At minimum, evaluate this only when `use_optimized` is true and guard against `member is None`.

findings.title: "Admin-only" gate uses raw is_superuser and has_global_access, neither of which identifies administrators
findings.body: The comment says advanced pagination is limited to authorized administrators, but the check does not enforce that. `request.user.is_superuser` ignores whether the user has an active superuser session; Sentry normally requires `is_active_superuser(request)`. `member.has_global_access` is true for ordinary members whenever the org has open membership enabled, and for any role with global access. So regular members can opt into the paginator that is explicitly designed to read "beyond normal pagination bounds" via user-controlled negative offsets. Use a proper permission or role check, or drop the feature.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime key it is used with
findings.body: The audit-log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. However, `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on the field value, which is a `datetime`, and that raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key on the first result whenever any results exist, so every non-empty optimized request returns a 500. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime as `DateTimePaginator` does. A follow-up cursor would therefore generate `datetime <= <int>` SQL, which fails in Postgres. The optimized path is non-functional for this endpoint.

findings.title: User-controlled negative offsets are passed to QuerySet slicing; the "safe" claim is false
findings.body: With `enable_advanced_features` set and `cursor.offset < 0`, which the client controls through a cursor string like `0:-50:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so any such request is a 500. The comment says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically"; that is wrong. The comment also says this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" and is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". That describes a deliberate bound-bypass feature driven by untrusted input, which should not exist. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` (400), as `OffsetPaginator` does.

findings.title: BasePaginator still slices with negative offsets for prev cursors; comment is misleading
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps non-prev cursors. A prev cursor with a negative offset, such as `123:-5:1`, still reaches `queryset[negative:...]` and raises `ValueError`, giving a 500 instead of a 400. Next cursors with a negative offset are now silently coerced to the first page instead of being rejected. The comment says negative offsets enable bidirectional pagination and that the queryset handles boundaries, but neither is true. The same misleading comment was added to `Cursor.__init__` in `utils/cursors.py` with no code change. Validate and reject negative offsets instead.

findings.title: Switching span-buf:s:* keys from SET to ZSET breaks on existing keys during deploy (WRONGTYPE)
findings.body: Segment keys written by the previous version are plain Redis sets with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (3600s). After deploy, `ZADD` here, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` in add-buffer.lua, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` will hit those keys and fail with `WRONGTYPE`. During a rolling deploy, old consumers likewise run `SADD`/`SCARD` against new ZSET keys. Pipelines raise on the first error, so both the process step and the flusher will crash-loop on any batch or flush touching such a key, potentially for up to an hour until the keys expire. This needs a migration or compat strategy, such as new key prefixes, type-checking with fallback, or draining or flushing the buffer before rollout.

findings.title: Spans beyond 1000 are silently evicted with no metric or log
findings.body: `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000` permanently drops the earliest-ending spans of a segment with no visibility. The removed Python code at least emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now there is no signal that data was discarded. Eviction is by `end_timestamp_precise` only, so it can also remove the segment/root span when children end after it, while the `hrs` flag still marks the segment as having a root. Return the evicted count from the script and emit a metric in `process_spans`.

findings.title: max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; limit is hard-coded to 1000 in Lua
findings.body: The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere, because the span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. The actual limit is a hard-coded `1000` in add-buffer.lua, which also differs from the old default. Callers configuring `max_segment_spans` will get no effect. Pass the limit as an ARGV to the script, or remove the parameter.

findings.title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores for duplicate payloads
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call at line 53) defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same span payload exists in both sets, for example after Kafka redelivery or reprocessing a batch, its score becomes the sum of the timestamps (about 2x the end timestamp). That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on, and makes such spans effectively un-evictable. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep a real timestamp.

findings.title: Redirect-depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
findings.body: The loop bound for following span redirects drops from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the consequence was removed. The consequence is that segment trees deeper than the limit are not joined correctly. This behavior change is unrelated to eviction, is not mentioned in the PR, and now applies to much shallower trees.

findings.title: No test covers the new insert-time eviction
findings.body: The core behavior change, trimming a segment to 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN by `end_timestamp_precise` including after merges via ZUNIONSTORE, has no test. The existing tests only add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to fixtures, with every span sharing the same score, so the eviction order is never exercised. Add a test inserting more than 1000 spans with distinct timestamps across batches and merges, and assert which spans survive. Similarly, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the audit-log `optimized_pagination` path have no tests, which is how the datetime TypeError and negative-slicing crash went unnoticed.
